newsitem.title: FRANCE: TWA jetliner downed by U.S. missile, Salinger says.
newsitem.headline: TWA jetliner downed by U.S. missile, Salinger says.

text.p: Former White House adviser Pierre Salinger said on Friday that a U.S. Navy missile accidentally shot down the TWA airliner which crashed off New York in July killing all 230 people aboard.

Salinger said in a television interview that he had been given a document by an agent of the U.S. Secret Service which said the airliner had entered an area where the U.S. Navy was carrying out missile tests.
"The airliner was not the target of an attack...It was shot down by a military missile during a test," he told French television LCI.
Salinger said military officials in charge of the test had conducted it at an altitude of 13,000 feet in the belief that all aircraft in the area were flying at 21,000 feet.
The officials were unaware that TWA flight 800 had taken off late from New York and was flying lower than its scheduled altitude to steer clear of another aircraft, he said.
The airport control tower, in "a tragic error," failed to inform the Navy, Salinger said.
"There is a lot of proof for the document. I have since talked to several individuals who have upheld what the agent said," he said. "The truth must come out."
In Washington on Thursday night, a Navy spokesman at the Pentagon denied that a U.S. missile had accidentally brought down the Boeing 747 jumbo jet.
He pointed out that the U.S. military, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the National Transportation Safety Board had all rejected similar suggestions in the past.
A spokesman in New York for the FBI, which has been investigating the crash, also denied the suggestion on Thursday night.

"We are not familiar with what Mr Salinger has said...Our investigation so far has not revealed any evidence that a so-called friendly fire situation brought down TWA flight 800," said Joe Valiquette, the FBI spokesman.
Salinger, 71, was press spokesman for the late president John F. Kennedy and later Paris bureau chief for the U.S. television network ABC.
He initially disclosed the document to some 100 airline officials from 20 countries attending a meeting in the French Mediterranean resort of Cannes.
He said he had passed on his information to an unspecified U.S. television network which did not broadcast it. He accused the U.S. government of clamping a news blackout on the crash.

Investigators are still dredging the seabed off Long Island for evidence to explain the crash. They have established that a fuel tank exploded but not what set off the blast and there has been no official verdict on the disaster.
A missile, a bomb and a mechanical fault have all been suggested.
